opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a very natural comparison, but I'd frame it a little differently. CUDA's success wasn't just about the software itself. It came from many years of persistence: we kept investing even when the market wasn't obvious, we made it easy for developers to get started, and over time a whole ecosystem of libraries, tools, courses, and researchers grew around it. That ecosystem is what really made it hard to replace.

With Cosmos and Nemotron, the goal is similar in spirit. We want to lower the barrier for developers. Take physical AI. If you're a robotics startup or an autonomous driving team, building a world foundation model from scratch is extremely expensive. You need huge amounts of video data, a curation pipeline, tokenizers, and a lot of compute for training. Most teams can't afford that. So we build these foundation models, release them openly with permissive licenses, and let people post-train them for their own robots, their own cameras, their own environments. Nemotron plays a similar role on the language and reasoning side.

Will they become "the next CUDA"? Honestly, it's too early to say, and I don't think we should be arrogant about it. The AI model landscape moves much faster than the GPU programming landscape did. There are many strong open models from other companies and from the academic community, and that's healthy. A model can be state of the art today and surpassed in six months. So the moat can't be just one model checkpoint.

What I think can last is the full stack and the community. That means the data pipeline, the tokenizers, the evaluation tools, the post-training recipes, the integration with simulation like Omniverse, and the fact that developers can trust we'll keep improving it year after year. If developers build their workflows on top of it and find that it really saves them time, then an ecosystem can form, the same way it did with CUDA.

So my view is this: the opportunity is there, especially in physical AI, because the field is still early and nobody has defined the standard yet. But it will take the same thing CUDA took, which is a long-term commitment and real usefulness to developers. That's what we're focusing on, rather than trying to declare victory.

r001.rationale: The response says NVIDIA kept investing when “the market wasn't obvious,” but does not clearly identify accelerated computing’s future importance as the uncertain bet.

r002.rationale: It says the lasting opportunity is the “full stack and the community” and that the moat cannot be “just one model checkpoint,” clearly framing the CUDA equivalent as more than an individual model.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, and I want to be honest about it rather than just cheer for my own team.

CUDA succeeded for reasons that are hard to replicate. It wasn't that CUDA was the best programming model on day one. It was that NVIDIA kept investing in it for almost two decades when it made no money, the hardware and the software co-evolved together, and an entire generation of researchers learned to write their code on it. Every paper, every library, every graduate student built on top of it. By the time anyone noticed it was a moat, the moat was already very deep. The lock-in came from the ecosystem, not from the API.

So when people ask whether Cosmos or Nemotron can do the same thing, the first thing I say is that the mechanism has to be different. Models are not like a programming interface. A model is something you can replace. If a better open model comes out next month, people switch. There is no code you have to rewrite. So the stickiness of a single model is close to zero, and I don't think we should pretend otherwise.

What can be sticky is the layer around the model. With Cosmos, the bet is on physical AI, on robots, on autonomous vehicles, on simulation. In that world the hard part is not the transformer. The hard part is the data pipeline, the tokenizers for video, the simulation loop, the way you generate synthetic data and close the loop with the real robot. If we build that whole stack and people start training and evaluating their robots on it, then you get something closer to a CUDA effect, where the value is in the workflow and the tooling and the accumulated know-how, not in any one checkpoint.

With Nemotron, I see it more as a way to keep the open ecosystem healthy and to make sure NVIDIA understands, from the inside, what frontier training really costs and really needs. That feeds back into the hardware. It's useful even if Nemotron never becomes the default model for anyone.

So my honest assessment: the chance that either becomes a CUDA-style moat by itself is low. The chance that the physical AI stack as a whole, with Cosmos as one piece, becomes a place where a lot of the industry standardizes, I think that's real, but it requires years of boring, patient investment, and it requires us to be genuinely open, because the moment people feel trapped they will route around you. CUDA earned trust before it earned lock-in. We would have to do the same.

r001.rationale: The response says NVIDIA invested in CUDA for nearly two decades while it made no money, but does not say the future importance of accelerated computing was uncertain.

r002.rationale: It says a CUDA-like effect could come from the physical AI stack as a whole, with Cosmos as one piece, rather than from either model alone.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s possible, but I would separate adoption from the kind of ecosystem success CUDA represents. For Cosmos or Nemotron, having a strong model is an important starting point. The bigger question is whether developers build on it, adapt it to their own problems, and keep coming back as their needs evolve.

CUDA’s strength is not just a particular capability; it’s the investment people make in tools, software, and expertise around it. To achieve something similar, Cosmos or Nemotron would need to become a foundation that other people can reliably build businesses on. That requires useful capabilities, accessible tooling, and a clear path from experimentation to deployment.

So I see the potential, but I wouldn’t assume the same trajectory. The model space moves quickly, and developers have many choices. The real test is whether an ecosystem develops around these models that delivers lasting value beyond any single release.

r001.rationale: The response discusses investment in tools, software, and expertise around CUDA, but does not characterize NVIDIA’s investment as a bet made while the importance of accelerated computing was uncertain.

r002.rationale: It says Cosmos or Nemotron would need an ecosystem, but does not suggest that a CUDA equivalent today could be a combination of technology stacks rather than an individual model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s possible, but I wouldn’t assume they’ll follow the same path. CUDA’s success is about more than the technology—it’s about becoming a foundation that developers build on. For Cosmos or Nemotron, the question is whether they can become that kind of foundation in their respective areas.

Cosmos has an opportunity around physical AI: helping people develop systems that understand and interact with the physical world. Nemotron has an opportunity around models that developers can adapt and build into applications. In both cases, strong capabilities are only the starting point. You also need useful tools, accessibility, and an ecosystem that keeps creating value.

So I see the potential, but it’s too early to call either one the next CUDA. That’s something you earn through sustained adoption.

r001.rationale: The response discusses CUDA’s success as a foundation, but does not characterize NVIDIA’s investment in CUDA as a bet made while accelerated computing’s future importance was uncertain.

r002.rationale: It mentions tools and ecosystems alongside Cosmos and Nemotron, but does not suggest that CUDA’s successor may be a combination of technology stacks rather than an individual model.
